item.title: Government boosts groundwater drilling capacity to address water shortages
item.description: Families in 86 communities across Fiji are still waiting for water supply systems to be installed despite boreholes already being drilled, as the Government works to improve access to safe and reliable water in areas facing water shortages. The Ministry of Lands and Mineral Resources says increased funding has boosted drilling capacity from an average of 15 boreholes annually to 93 boreholes durin
item.content:encoded:
Families in 86 communities across Fiji are still waiting for water supply systems to be installed despite boreholes already being drilled, as the Government works to improve access to safe and reliable water in areas facing water shortages.

The Ministry of Lands and Mineral Resources says increased funding has boosted drilling capacity from an average of 15 boreholes annually to 93 boreholes during the 2024-2026 period, with 80 boreholes targeted for the 2025-2026 financial year.

The Ministry says it is working with the Ministry of Rural and Maritime Development and Disaster Management to provide basic water supply systems to these communities while permanent water distribution systems are being pursued.

These temporary systems will include a submersible pump, a water storage tank and a centrally located community standpipe, allowing residents to collect water for drinking, cooking and other essential household needs.

The Ministry says the Government continues to strengthen efforts to assist communities outside the Water Authority of Fiji network, particularly drought-prone areas, remote rural settlements and maritime islands where surface water sources are inadequate, contaminated or unavailable.

The Ministry says through the Groundwater Assistance Programme, the Government provides assistance with groundwater surveys, drilling and development to communities experiencing water shortages.

The programme focuses on some of the driest areas on Fiji's major islands and smaller islands where groundwater is the most practical source of freshwater.

The Ministry says 232 boreholes have been successfully drilled since 2015, with 88 of these subsequently completed with water reticulation systems.

It says demand for groundwater development has continued to increase as more communities become aware of the programme and climate change contributes to more frequent and prolonged droughts.

The programme, which began in the early 1980s, has assisted communities across Fiji, including many maritime islands.

The Ministry says the Government significantly increased funding for the programme in the 2024-2025 financial year, allowing three private drilling contractors to be engaged and increasing the capacity to reach more communities.

The Ministry says the Australia-Fiji Vuvale Partnership-funded Airborne Electromagnetic Geophysical Survey has also helped identify potential groundwater sources in water-scarce areas.

They say previously the Department relied on time-consuming ground investigations, which allowed surveys of only around 20 communities each year, however, w ith the new survey data, technical assessments and potential drilling locations can now be identified more efficiently in areas covered by the survey.

The Ministry says the Government is also continuing to assist communities facing water shortages through coordinated efforts led by the National Disaster Risk Management Office.

Meanwhile, the Ministry is encouraging communities experiencing ongoing water shortages, including residents of Ellington Settlement in Rakiraki, to submit formal requests for assistance as soon as possible.

Requests must be submitted to the Director Mineral Resources or the Ministry's Permanent Secretary and should clearly explain the water problems being faced.

They must also include the contact details of a community representative and a supporting letter from the relevant Provincial Office, through the Provincial Administrator or District Officer, confirming the authenticity of the request.

The Ministry says this will allow communities' water needs to be assessed and considered under the Groundwater Assistance Programme.

item.title: Police investigate firecracker incident at Davuilevu home, no one questioned yet
item.description: Navitalai Naivalurua · 12/11/2026 Police are investigating an incident in which some children allegedly threw firecrackers at a home in Davuilevu where a family was celebrating Diwali.
item.content:encoded:
Navitalai Naivalurua · 12/11/2026

Police are investigating an incident in which some children allegedly threw firecrackers at a home in Davuilevu where a family was celebrating Diwali.

Police confirm that no one has been questioned yet in relation to the incident.

Meanwhile, serious concerns have been raised about the behaviour of some children during Diwali celebrations this year, with two videos widely shared on social media appearing to show children involved in the incidents.

A video shared by a family from Davuilevu shows children throwing firecrackers while the family was celebrating Diwali at their home.

This has raised serious concerns about the safety and security of families celebrating religious occasions with their loved ones.

The video shows family members sharing a basin of kava when firecrackers were thrown into their house.

The family has reported the incident to the Nakasi Police Station. However, they say no action was taken and Police did not respond to their report.

There was also an incident in Cunningham Stage 4, where some children allegedly threw firecrackers into a shop.

item.title: Water shortage forces Tavua farmer to stop vegetable farming
item.description: A farmer from Viti Vanua Settlement in Tavua says the ongoing water shortage has forced his family to stop vegetable farming, leaving them struggling with the rising cost of buying vegetables. Speaking to fijivillage News, Satish Kumar says a bundle of beans, which was $3, is now $7.
item.content:encoded:
A farmer from Viti Vanua Settlement in Tavua says the ongoing water shortage has forced his family to stop vegetable farming, leaving them struggling with the rising cost of buying vegetables.

Speaking to fijivillage News, Satish Kumar says a bundle of beans, which was $3, is now $7.

Kumar says they currently rely on borehole water, but the supply is limited, forcing them to carefully manage their daily water use.

He says tap water is only available three times a week for a few hours, making it difficult for them to carry out farming activities.

Kumar says they are now only able to focus on sugarcane farming due to the water shortage.

He says the prolonged dry weather is also affecting livestock farmers, as there is not enough grass for their animals to graze on.

Kumar adds that the price of millmix, which is used as livestock feed, has increased from $5 to $17.

He says families are storing whatever water they can for future use.

Kumar is concerned that families may end up buying bottled water, which would place further financial pressure on them.

He says he currently receives two cartons of bottled water from his employer, Fiji Water, which helps his family manage the situation.

Kumar says farmers are struggling with the ongoing dry conditions and is calling on the government to provide financial assistance through grants to help affected farmers cope with the rising costs.

item.title: Fiji Airways may not replace some departing staff as AI improves efficiency “ Scurrah
item.description: Fiji Airways may not need to replace some employees who leave the airline as it introduces artificial intelligence to improve efficiency and reduce high operating costs. Speaking on fijivillage Straight Talk with Vijay Narayan, Fiji Airways CEO and Managing Director Paul Scurrah says the airline employs about 2,200 people and is reviewing its staffing levels and organisational structure as part of
item.content:encoded:
Fiji Airways may not need to replace some employees who leave the airline as it introduces artificial intelligence to improve efficiency and reduce high operating costs.

Speaking on fijivillage Straight Talk with Vijay Narayan, Fiji Airways CEO and Managing Director Paul Scurrah says the airline employs about 2,200 people and is reviewing its staffing levels and organisational structure as part of efforts to achieve financial sustainability.

Scurrah acknowledges that some areas of the business may have more staff than needed and says the airline is looking at ways to operate more efficiently.

He says Fiji Airways still relies heavily on manual processes and is investing in technology to improve productivity.

Scurrah says artificial intelligence could take over some routine tasks, allowing employees to focus on more meaningful work.

However, he acknowledges that as technology improves, the airline may not need to fill some vacancies when employees leave.

Scurrah stresses that this does not mean Fiji Airways is planning widespread job cuts because of artificial intelligence.

He says any decisions affecting employees will be made carefully and respectfully.

Meanwhile, Scurrah says Fiji Airways plans to introduce an additional 125,000 passenger seats in 2027, which is expected to increase operational demand and provide opportunities to make better use of its existing workforce.

He says the staffing review forms part of wider cost-reduction efforts across the airline, including property rentals, procurement and catering.

Scurrah stresses that Fiji Airways must become financially sustainable while continuing to provide reliable services to its customers.
